claims.text: CrMnFeCoNi is a chemically disordered high-entropy alloy.
The predictive approach can accurately identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity CrMnFeCoNi-based alloys.
Chemical disorder causes soft phonon modes to emerge in CrMnFeCoNi-based alloys.
Local lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations lower the energies of phonon modes.
Soft phonon modes play a decisive role in enhancing phonon scattering.
Near-equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi can exist as a single-phase, intrinsically disordered alloy.
Chemically induced lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations produce localized phonon states.
Chemical disorder produces mass and force-constant fluctuations that reduce phonon lifetimes.
Elemental or chemical fluctuations can induce lattice distortion and strain fluctuations.
Lattice distortion and strain fluctuations strengthen phonon scattering and reduce lattice thermal conductivity.
The approach will achieve a correlation of approximately 80% or better between predicted and measured soft-mode energies.
Detection of soft modes within 10% of their predicted energies would support the predictive approach.
Failure to detect the predicted modes or deviations exceeding 10% would falsify the hypothesis.
A correlation below approximately 80% between soft-mode characteristics and reduced thermal conductivity would falsify the hypothesis.
Conventional Debye or perturbative models omit detailed chemical-disorder effects and consequently have higher lattice-thermal-conductivity prediction errors.
The approach is applicable to near-equiatomic or slightly tuned high-entropy alloys when chemical disorder dominates phonon behavior.
The approach may not apply when grain boundaries or secondary-phase precipitates dominate thermal transport.
Soft-mode scattering signals may overlap with other scattering phenomena, complicating their isolation.
The quantitative improvement over existing predictive models has not yet been established.
